title: VI. “I Am Coming, Too!”
paragraphs: But Dmitri Fyodorovitch was racing down the road. Mokroe was a little over twenty versts away, but Andrey’s three horses ran so fast that they could cover it in an hour and a quarter. The speed brought Mitya back to life. The air was cool and fresh, and large stars stood out in the sky. It was the very night, and maybe the very hour, when Alyosha threw himself down on the earth and swore in a rapture to love it forever and ever.

Everything in Mitya’s soul was in confusion, pure confusion. Many things were goading his heart. Yet at that moment his whole being longed for her, his queen, and he was flying to see her for the last time. One thing I can say for certain: his heart did not waver for a single instant. People may not believe me when I say this, but the jealous lover felt no jealousy at all toward the new rival who seemed to have sprung out of the ground. Any other man who turned up would have made him jealous at once, and he might well have stained his violent hands with blood again. But as he flew through the night, he felt no envy and not even any hostility toward the man who had been her first lover.... True, he had not yet laid eyes on him.

“Here there was no room for dispute: it was her right and his. This was her first love, and after five years she had not forgotten it. So for five whole years she had loved only him, and I—what am I to her? What right do I have? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! What am I now? Now it’s all over, apart from the officer—even if he had never turned up, it would all be over ...”

These words would roughly have put his feelings into speech, if he had been in any state to reason. But he was not. His plan of action had not been reasoned out. It had sprung from feeling the moment Fenya spoke, and he had taken it up in a flash, with everything that followed from it. And still, despite his resolve, his soul was in turmoil, an agonizing turmoil. The resolve gave him no peace. Too much lay behind him, and it tormented him. At times it struck him as strange that he had written his own death sentence with pen and paper—“I punish myself”—and that the paper was lying in his pocket, ready, and the pistol was loaded, and he had already settled how he would meet the first warm ray of “golden-haired Phœbus” next morning.

Still, he could not shake off the past, all that he had left behind and that tortured him. He felt this wretchedly, and the thought sank into his heart like despair. For one moment he had the urge to stop Andrey, jump out of the cart, pull out his loaded pistol and finish everything without waiting for dawn. But the moment passed like a spark. The horses galloped on, “devouring space.” As he got closer to his goal, the thought of her, only of her, filled his soul more and more and drove out the terrible pictures that had haunted it. Oh, how he longed to see her, if only for a moment, if only from far off!

“She’s with _him_ now,” he thought. “Now I’ll see what she looks like beside him, her first love, and that’s all I ask.” Never before had this woman, who had such a fateful hold on his life, roused such love in his breast. It was a new, unknown feeling, which surprised even him, a feeling so tender that it was almost worship, a wish to efface himself before her. “I will efface myself!” he said, in a surge of almost hysterical ecstasy.

They had been galloping for nearly an hour. Mitya said nothing. Andrey, who was usually a talkative peasant, had not spoken either. He seemed afraid to, and only kept whipping up his three lean but spirited bays. Then suddenly Mitya cried out in horrible anxiety:
“Andrey! What if they’re asleep?”
The idea hit him like a blow. It had never crossed his mind until now.
“They may well be in bed by now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
Mitya frowned as if in pain. Yes, of course ... here he was rushing there ... with such feelings ... and they were asleep ... she was asleep, perhaps, there too.... Anger rose in his heart.
“Drive on, Andrey! Whip them up! Look alive!” he cried, beside himself.
“But maybe they’re not in bed!” Andrey went on after a pause. “Timofey said there was a whole crowd of them there—”
“At the station?”
“Not the posting-station, but Plastunov’s, the inn, where they hire out horses, too.”
“I know the place. So there’s a crowd, you say? How is that? Who are they?” cried Mitya, badly shaken by this news.

“Well, Timofey said they’re all gentlefolk. Two are from our town—who, I can’t say—and two more are strangers, and maybe there are others. I didn’t ask in particular. They’ve started playing cards, so Timofey said.”
“Cards?”
“So they may not be in bed if they’re at cards. It’s probably not even eleven.”
“Faster, Andrey! Faster!” Mitya cried again, in a nervous voice.
“Can I ask you something, sir?” said Andrey after a pause. “Only I’m afraid you’ll be angry, sir.”
“What is it?”

“Well, Fenya threw herself at your feet a while ago and begged you not to hurt her mistress, or somebody else, either ... so you see, sir— I’m the one driving you there ... forgive me, sir, it’s my conscience ... maybe it’s foolish of me to bring it up—”
Mitya suddenly grabbed him by the shoulders from behind.
“Are you a driver?” he asked wildly.
“Yes, sir.”

“Then you know a man has to give way. What would you say of a driver who wouldn’t give way to anybody, who just drove on and crushed people? No, a driver mustn’t run people down. You can’t run down a human being. You can’t wreck people’s lives. And if you have wrecked a life—punish yourself.... If you’ve only wrecked, if you’ve only ruined somebody’s life—punish yourself and go away.”
The words burst out of Mitya in something close to hysteria. Andrey was astonished, but he kept the conversation going.

“That’s right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you’re quite right. A man mustn’t be crushed or tormented, nor any creature, because God made every one of them. Take a horse, say. Some folks, even among us drivers, drive any way they like. Nothing holds them back, they just push the horse on.”

“To hell?” Mitya broke in, and let out his short, abrupt laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” and he grabbed him by the shoulders again, “tell me, what do you think, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not?”

“I can’t say, darling, it depends on you, because you are ... you see, sir, when the Son of God was nailed to the Cross and died, He went down to hell from the Cross and set free all the sinners who were suffering there. And the devil groaned, because he thought he’d get no more sinners in hell. And God said to him then, ‘Do not groan, for you shall have all the mighty of the earth, the rulers, the chief judges and the rich, and you shall be filled up as you have been in all the ages till I come again.’ Those were His very words ...”
“A peasant legend! Wonderful! Whip up the left horse, Andrey!”

“So you see, sir, who hell is meant for,” said Andrey, whipping up the left horse, “but you’re like a little child ... that’s how we think of you ... and you may be hot-tempered, sir, but God will forgive you for your kind heart.”
“And you, Andrey, do you forgive me?”
“What have I got to forgive you, sir? You’ve never done me any harm.”
“No, for everyone, for everyone, you alone here on the road—will you forgive me for everyone? Speak, simple peasant heart!”
“Oh, sir! I’m afraid of driving you, the way you talk is so strange.”
But Mitya did not hear him. He was praying wildly and muttering to himself.

“Lord, take me as I am, with all my lawlessness, and do not condemn me. Let me slip past Your judgment ... do not condemn me, for I have condemned myself. Do not condemn me, for I love You, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love You. If You send me to hell, I shall love You there, and from there I shall cry out that I love You forever and ever.... But let me love to the end.... Here and now, for just five hours ... until the first light of Your day ... for I love the queen of my soul ... I love her and I cannot help loving her. You see my whole heart.... I shall gallop up, I shall fall down before her and say, ‘You are right to go your way and leave me. Farewell, and forget your victim ... never trouble yourself over me!’”
“Mokroe!” cried Andrey, pointing ahead with his whip.

Out of the pale darkness of the night rose a solid black mass of buildings, dropped, it seemed, onto the vast plain. Mokroe was a village of two thousand people, but at that hour all of them were asleep, and only a few scattered lights still twinkled.
“Drive on, Andrey, I’m coming!” Mitya exclaimed in a fever.
“They’re not asleep,” said Andrey again, pointing his whip at the Plastunovs’ inn at the edge of the village. All six of its windows on the street were blazing with light.
“They’re not asleep,” Mitya repeated with joy. “Faster, Andrey! Gallop! Come in with a dash! Make the bells ring! Let everybody know I’ve come. I’m coming! I’m coming, too!”
Andrey lashed his worn-out horses into a gallop, swept up with a dash, and pulled his steaming, panting team to a stop at the high front steps.
Mitya sprang from the cart just as the innkeeper, who was heading for bed, looked out from the steps to see who had arrived.
“Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?”
The innkeeper bent forward and peered, then ran down the steps and hurried up to his guest with cringing delight.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, your honor! Is it really you again?”

Trifon Borissovitch was a stocky, healthy peasant of middle height, with a rather fat face. His look was stern and hard, especially toward the peasants of Mokroe. But he could put on the most cringing face imaginable when he smelled some profit in it. He dressed in the Russian way, in a shirt that buttoned at the side and a coat with full skirts. He had put by a good sum, yet he was forever dreaming of rising in the world. More than half the peasants were in his clutches, and everyone in the district owed him money. He bought and leased land from the neighboring landowners, and the peasants worked it to pay off debts they could never be rid of. He was a widower with four grown daughters. One was already a widow and lived at the inn with her two children, his grandchildren, working for him like a charwoman. Another had married a petty official, and in one of the inn’s rooms, among the family photographs on the wall, hung a small photograph of this official in uniform and official epaulettes. The two younger daughters wore fashionable blue or green dresses, tight in the back and with trains a yard long, on Church holidays or when they paid calls. Yet the next morning they would be up at dawn as always, sweeping the rooms with a birch broom, emptying slops and cleaning up after the lodgers.

For all the thousands of roubles he had saved, Trifon Borissovitch dearly loved to empty a drunken guest’s pockets. He remembered that less than a month before, in just twenty-four hours, he had taken two or even three hundred roubles from Dmitri, when Dmitri came on his spree with Grushenka. So he gave him an eager welcome now, scenting his prey the instant Mitya drove up to the steps.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, so we see you again!”
“Hold on, Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began, “first of all, where is she?”
“Agrafena Alexandrovna?” The innkeeper understood at once and gave Mitya’s face a sharp look. “She’s here, too ...”
“Who’s with her? Who?”

“Some strangers. One is an official, a gentleman, a Pole by the sound of him. He’s the one who sent the horses from here to fetch her. And there’s another with him, a friend of his or a traveling companion, who can tell. They’re in civilian clothes.”
“Well, are they feasting? Have they money?”
“A poor sort of feast! Nothing to brag about, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“Nothing to brag about? And who are the others?”

“Two gentlemen from the town.... They’ve come back from Tcherny and put up here. One is quite a young gentleman, a relation of Mr. Miüsov, it must be, but I’ve forgotten his name ... and I expect you know the other as well, a gentleman by the name of Maximov. He’s been on a pilgrimage, he says, to the monastery in the town. He’s traveling with this young relation of Mr. Miüsov.”
“Is that all?”
“Yes.”
“Listen, Trifon Borissovitch, hold on. Tell me the main thing: what about her? How is she?”
“Oh, she only just got here. She’s sitting with them.”
“Is she cheerful? Is she laughing?”
“No, I don’t think she’s laughing much. She’s sitting there rather bored. She’s combing the young gentleman’s hair.”
“The Pole—the officer?”
“He isn’t young, and he isn’t an officer, either. Not him, sir. I mean the young gentleman who’s Mr. Miüsov’s relation ... I’ve forgotten his name.”
“Kalganov.”
“That’s the one, Kalganov!”
“All right. I’ll see for myself. Are they playing cards?”
“They were, but they’ve given it up. They’ve had tea, and the official gentleman called for liqueurs.”
“Hold on, Trifon Borissovitch, hold on, my good soul, I’ll see for myself. Now answer me one more thing: are the gypsies here?”
“No gypsies for you now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The authorities drove them off. But there are Jews in the village who play the cymbals and the fiddle, and we could send for them. They’d come.”
“Send for them. Yes, send for them!” cried Mitya. “And get the girls together the way you did before, Marya above all, and Stepanida, and Arina, too. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!”

“Oh, for money like that I can rouse the whole village, even though they’re asleep by now. But are the peasants here worth such kindness, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or the girls, either? Throwing away that much on such coarse, rude people! What’s the use of giving a peasant a cigar, the stinking ruffian! And the girls are all lousy. Besides, I’ll get my own daughters up for nothing, never mind that sum. They’ve only just gone to bed—I’ll give them a kick and make them sing for you. The other day you gave the peasants champagne to drink, e—ech!”

Whatever sympathy Trifon Borissovitch pretended to feel for Mitya, on that last visit he had hidden half a dozen bottles of champagne, and he had picked up a hundred-rouble note from under the table and kept it.
“Trifon Borissovitch, last time I was here I sent more than a thousand flying. Do you remember?”
“Flying it went. How could I forget? You must have left three thousand behind.”
“Well, I’ve come to do the same again, do you see?”
And he pulled out his roll of banknotes and held it up right in front of the innkeeper’s nose.

“Now listen and remember. In an hour the wine will get here, with savories, pies and sweets—bring it all up at once. And that box Andrey has is to come up at once as well. Open it and pour champagne right away. And the girls, we need the girls, Marya most of all.”
He turned to the cart and took out the box of pistols.
“Here, Andrey, let’s settle. Here are fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka ... for your willingness, for your love.... Remember Karamazov!”
“I’m afraid, sir,” Andrey faltered. “Give me five roubles extra, but I won’t take more than that. Trifon Borissovitch, you’re my witness. Forgive my foolish words ...”

“What are you afraid of?” asked Mitya, looking him over. “Well, go to the devil, if that’s how it is!” he cried, flinging him five roubles. “Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me up quietly and let me have a look at them first, so they won’t see me. Where are they? In the blue room?”

Trifon Borissovitch gave Mitya a wary look, but at once did as he was told. He took him into the passage and went by himself into the first big room, next to the one where the guests sat, and carried away the light. Then he led Mitya in on tiptoe and set him in a dark corner, where he could watch the company freely without being seen. But Mitya did not look for long. In fact he could not see them at all. He saw her. His heart pounded, and everything went dark before his eyes.

She sat sideways to the table in a low chair, and next to her on the sofa was the pretty youth, Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, while he, who looked annoyed and would not look at her, was saying something loudly to Maximov, who sat across the table facing Grushenka. Maximov was roaring with laughter at something. On the sofa sat _he_, and on a chair beside the sofa sat the other stranger. The man on the sofa was leaning back and smoking a pipe. Mitya got the impression of a stoutish, short little man with a broad face, who was plainly angry about something. His friend, the other stranger, struck Mitya as remarkably tall, but he could make out nothing more. He caught his breath. He could not stand it for a minute. He set the pistol-case down on a chest and, his heart pounding and a chill running through him, walked straight into the blue room to face them all.
“Aie!” shrieked Grushenka, who was the first to see him.
